strengths: TASTE addresses a relevant bottleneck in joint speech–text modeling: mismatched sequence lengths. Using ASR-initialized cross-attention to aggregate acoustic information into text-aligned representations is a plausible and useful design.

Table 1 provides evidence that TASTE retains information beyond text and speaker identity: emotion consistency improves from 0.47 to 0.67 and duration consistency from 0.36 to 0.73 over the text-only baseline, at a reported bitrate of approximately 190 bits/s.

The 1B LoRA-adapted models achieve encouraging StoryCloze results and substantially outperform the reported S3-token LoRA baseline. Evaluating both discrete tokens and continuous embeddings also demonstrates some flexibility in the representation.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is not adequately validated. There are no ablations comparing shallow versus final-layer attention values, ASR initialization, ordinary pooling, explicit alignment, or alternative compression rates. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the proposed aggregation is necessary or whether improvements primarily reflect transcript conditioning and the pretrained reconstruction components.

The downstream comparisons do not isolate the effect of text alignment. Prior systems differ in backbone, training data, scale, and adaptation strategy, while the S3 LoRA baseline is insufficiently specified and performs near chance on SALMON. Matched-backbone, matched-data comparisons with stronger speech–text modeling strategies are needed. StoryCloze results also remain substantially below ASR+LLM: approximately 64 versus 73.5 on sSC and 89 versus 95.9 on tSC.

Claims about natural speech continuation and effective generation exceed the evaluation. Table 1 measures reconstruction, while Table 2 measures likelihood-based discrimination. Neither evaluates freely generated continuations, text–speech consistency during generation, or human judgments of naturalness and coherence. These are important omissions for a model intended to both listen and speak.

The compression comparison needs clearer accounting and qualification. TASTE reconstruction requires text and a speaker embedding, whereas SpeechTokenizer does not receive these side channels. The approximately 190-bit/s estimate lacks a derivation explaining the contribution of text, acoustic codes, and speaker information. Reconstruction is evaluated only on LibriTTS test-clean, without human listening tests or uncertainty estimates; UTMOS exceeding ground truth does not establish superior perceptual quality.

Computational efficiency is asserted rather than demonstrated. No measured sequence-length distributions, training throughput, memory use, inference latency, or end-to-end compute comparisons are provided. Shorter LLM sequences are promising, but the system also requires ASR, aggregation, autoregressive unit decoding, and waveform synthesis.

Important methodological and reproducibility details are missing. These include the selected shallow encoder layer, unit-decoder architecture, speech/text input fusion, latent-loss weights, SLM training duration, and precise likelihood scoring and normalization for both model variants. Equation 13 omits a text-prediction loss despite describing joint speech–text generation. The RVQ update rule and commitment-loss specification also need clarification.

The paper establishes equal sequence lengths by construction, but does not directly establish local acoustic–text correspondence. Unrestricted cross-attention can draw information from the entire utterance. Alignment analysis and robustness tests with imperfect transcripts would strengthen the central interpretation, particularly because high-quality ASR is assumed throughout.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: reducing speech sequence lengths to facilitate joint speech–text modeling. The ASR-initialized aggregation mechanism provides a plausible approach without requiring explicit temporal word alignments.

Table 1 provides evidence that the learned acoustic representation adds information beyond text and speaker conditioning: emotion consistency improves from 0.47 to 0.67 and duration consistency from 0.36 to 0.73.
The 1B LoRA-adapted models achieve promising StoryCloze results, outperforming the reported speech-model baselines, while retaining useful acoustic discrimination on several SALMON tasks.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not isolate the proposed mechanism's contribution. There are no ablations of shallow-value cross-attention, ASR initialization, word-level aggregation, or quantization capacity, and no matched comparison against simpler pooling or alignment approaches.

The main spoken-generation claims are unsupported by direct evaluation. SALMON and StoryCloze measure likelihood-based discrimination; reconstruction evaluates the tokenizer and decoder. Neither establishes the quality, coherence, or acoustic consistency of freely generated speech continuations.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently established. Previous systems differ in backbone, training data, and adaptation strategy, while the implementation and tuning of the S3 joint-modeling baseline are underspecified. Its near-chance SALMON performance makes stronger controlled comparisons particularly important. TASTE also receives explicit transcripts, so semantic gains cannot be attributed solely to improved acoustic representations.

The compression comparison needs clearer accounting and matched conditions. TASTE reconstruction requires text and a speaker embedding, whereas SpeechTokenizer does not receive these separate inputs. The approximately 190-bit/s figure lacks an explicit accounting formula covering all required information. Duration consistency is also substantially below four-layer SpeechTokenizer, 0.73 versus 0.82, qualifying the claimed comparable reconstruction performance.

Computational savings are asserted without measured training throughput, inference latency, memory, or total pipeline cost. Shorter LLM sequences are promising, but ASR, tokenization, and autoregressive unit decoding introduce costs that are not evaluated.

Important methodological details are missing. Equation 13 omits a text-prediction loss despite describing joint text–embedding modeling; loss weights, unit-decoder architecture, exact shallow layer, language-model training duration, and benchmark likelihood aggregation are not adequately specified. These omissions impede reproducibility and interpretation of the embedding variant.

Evaluation breadth and uncertainty are limited: reconstruction is tested only on LibriTTS test-clean, with no human listening study, ASR-error robustness analysis, or confidence intervals. UTMOS exceeding the ground-truth score does not establish superior perceptual fidelity. Overall, the results support a promising approach but fall short of substantiating the paper's broader effectiveness and efficiency claims.

strengths: TASTE addresses an important bottleneck in joint speech–text modeling: mismatched sequence lengths. ASR-initialized aggregation followed by residual quantization provides a plausible way to obtain compact, text-aligned acoustic representations without explicit temporal word alignments.

Table 1 provides evidence that TASTE preserves information beyond text: emotion consistency improves from 0.47 to 0.67 and duration consistency from 0.36 to 0.73 over the text-only reconstruction baseline, while maintaining low WER.
The 1B LoRA-adapted models achieve promising StoryCloze results and outperform the reported S3-token baseline. Exploring both discrete-token and continuous-embedding prediction is useful.
weaknesses: The central design choices are not validated through ablations. There are no controlled comparisons for shallow versus final-layer values, ASR initialization, word-level averaging, quantization settings, or text alignment versus simpler compression. Consequently, the experiments do not establish which proposed components cause the improvements.

The downstream comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. Previous systems differ in backbone, training data, scale, and adaptation strategy, while the S3 baseline's implementation and tuning are insufficiently described. A matched text-only adaptation baseline and controlled LoRA/full-finetuning comparisons are needed to support the claims about alignment and reduced catastrophic forgetting.

The evaluation does not substantiate the claimed ability to generate natural, coherent speech continuations. SALMON and StoryCloze measure likelihood-based discrimination; Table 1 evaluates reconstruction with supplied conditioning. There is no direct evaluation of freely generated continuations, human listening study, or generation-specific intelligibility and coherence assessment.

The bitrate comparison lacks explicit accounting for transcription and speaker-embedding side information. Although Table 1 separates systems by speaker conditioning, its headline compression comparison still involves different information budgets and reconstruction pipelines. Speaker similarity is particularly difficult to attribute to TASTE because the text-only baseline already achieves 0.82 versus TASTE's 0.84.

The claimed computational benefits are not measured. Shorter LLM sequences are promising, but there are no matched throughput, memory, latency, or training-cost results accounting for ASR, tokenization, and the autoregressive unit decoder.

Important implementation and evaluation details are missing: unit-decoder architecture, the selected shallow encoder layer, latent-loss weights, SLM training duration, and likelihood aggregation and normalization across text and speech outputs. Equation 13 also omits the text-prediction loss despite describing joint speech–text modeling. Continuous-embedding likelihood scoring is insufficiently specified.

Evidence for robustness is limited to English and clean read-speech reconstruction, with no ASR-error sensitivity analysis, confidence intervals, or repeated runs. Acoustic performance is mixed: TASTE trails stronger systems on several SALMON dimensions and remains below S3 on emotion and duration consistency. These results support a promising approach, but not the manuscript's broader claims of robustness and generalizability.

strengths: TASTE addresses a relevant problem: reducing speech–text sequence mismatch through transcript-conditioned aggregation and compact speech representations.

Reconstruction results provide evidence that the representation preserves useful paralinguistic information: duration consistency improves from 0.57 for text-only reconstruction to 0.91, and MUSHRA improves from 42.6 to 68.3.
The 1.3B TASLM reports substantial continuation improvements over TWIST and Spirit LM, alongside strong StoryCloze results, using parameter-efficient adaptation.

Evaluation includes objective metrics, human listening tests, acoustic and semantic benchmarks, and spoken question answering. The appendix supplies training details, evaluation prompts, and variability estimates.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently isolated. There are no controlled ablations of text alignment versus comparable-rate compression, shallow versus deep encoder features, attention design, or RVQ depth. Comparisons across different pretrained LMs and speech decoders cannot establish that alignment causes the gains; the S3 baseline alone is insufficient.

The approximately 150-bps claim lacks explicit accounting for all decoder inputs, including transcription and speaker embedding. Without separating speech-code bitrate from total transmitted information and specifying equivalent side information for baselines, the codec comparison is difficult to interpret. Reconstruction fidelity also remains below several baselines on WER, ViSQOL, and duration consistency.

Important implementation details remain unresolved. Algorithm 1 averages already-quantized embeddings but does not explain how the resulting averages acquire discrete RVQ codes. Aggregator and unit-decoder architectures, the selected shallow layer, embedding-loss weights, and SLM training duration are not adequately specified.

Equation 7 is mathematically incorrect as written: the stated Gaussian KL divergence requires a variance term sigma squared, whereas the equation uses sigma. This needs correction and confirmation of the implemented objective.

Likelihood evaluation is underspecified, particularly for the continuous-embedding model: the paper does not explain how text and speech likelihoods are combined or normalized. Because tokenization attends across the utterance, the evaluation should also explain how prompt–continuation boundaries are handled to prevent continuation information entering prompt representations.

Human evaluation uses only 20 utterances per method. Reported standard deviations do not establish statistical significance for small differences, such as human MOS 4.16 versus 4.00 for the matched cascade. That cascade also essentially matches semantic continuation performance, weakening claims of superiority over the underlying text-based pipeline.

Evidence for broad acoustic preservation and precise editing is limited. The embedding model scores 57.7 on SALMON versus 69.0 for expressive Spirit LM, with several acoustic categories near chance. Editing is illustrated qualitatively, and robustness to transcription errors is assumed rather than tested.

strengths: TASTE addresses a relevant problem: shortening speech representations and aligning them with text to simplify joint spoken language modeling. The reconstruction-trained aggregation mechanism is a plausible and useful design.

The reconstruction results provide evidence that TASTE preserves information beyond text: duration consistency improves from 0.57 to 0.91 and MUSHRA from 42.6 to 68.3 relative to the text-only baseline.

The downstream results are promising. With a 1.3B backbone and 45M fine-tuned parameters, TASLM substantially outperforms the evaluated TWIST and Spirit LM systems on continuation MOS and achieves strong StoryCloze results.

The evaluation includes objective metrics, human listening tests, acoustic and semantic benchmarks, and spoken question answering. The appendix supplies additional results, variability estimates, and evaluation prompts.
weaknesses: The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the central contribution. There are no ablations of the shallow-value/deep-key attention design, reconstruction objective, quantization configuration, or word-level aggregation. A matched forced-alignment pooling baseline would help establish whether learned aggregation offers an advantage over simpler text-aligned representations. The S3 baseline alone cannot resolve these questions.

The comparisons confound tokenization with backbone, training procedure, and speech synthesis components. TASLM uses LLaMA3.2 and CosyVoice, whereas prominent baselines use different language models and decoders. The matched cascade is essentially tied on GPT-4o scores (3.16 versus 3.15), has higher UTMOS (4.25 versus 4.22), and trails only modestly on human MOS (4.00 versus 4.16). These results do not convincingly establish that joint modeling improves over the simpler pipeline.

The approximately 150-bps claim lacks a transparent accounting of all information required for decoding. Reconstruction also requires text and a speaker embedding, but their contribution to the reported bitrate is not clearly specified. Comparisons against waveform codecs therefore need explicit side-information accounting and matched rate–distortion analysis. TASTE also sacrifices fidelity: WER, ViSQOL, and duration consistency are worse than the S3 reference.

The human evaluation uses only 20 distinct samples per method. Although standard deviations are provided, there are no paired confidence intervals or significance tests supporting the claimed superiority over the cascade. Multiple ratings per utterance do not replace broader utterance coverage, particularly for the small 0.16 MOS difference.

Text-length alignment does not by itself demonstrate local acoustic alignment: each query can attend across the utterance. The editing evidence is primarily qualitative, without aggregate measurements of targeted changes and effects on untouched words. Moreover, Appendix A.2 requires word grouping, averaging, and replication to address tokenizer mismatch, qualifying the claim that alignment removes heuristic processing.

Acoustic modeling remains comparatively weak. TASLM obtains 57.7–60.8 on SALMON versus 69.0 for Spirit LM Expressive; the embedding variant is at or below chance on room and background conditions. The combined SALMON/StoryCloze average obscures this tradeoff, and no matched text-only likelihood baseline establishes how much semantic performance comes from the speech representation.

Technical specification and reproducibility are incomplete. Equation (7) uses sigma rather than sigma squared in the Gaussian KL variance term, inconsistent with the stated distributions. The manuscript also omits important architecture dimensions, loss weights, language-model training duration, decoding settings, and the precise likelihood-scoring procedure for continuous embeddings. The advertised code/model links are absent from the supplied manuscript. These gaps prevent checking whether the implementation supports the stated formulation.

strengths: TASTE addresses a meaningful problem: aligning speech representations with text tokens to simplify joint spoken language modeling. The reconstruction-trained aggregation mechanism is a promising design.
Reconstruction results demonstrate useful information beyond text: duration consistency improves from 0.57 to 0.91 and MUSHRA from 42.6 to 68.3 relative to the text-only baseline.

The small TASLM models achieve strong reported continuation results against TWIST and Spirit LM, with evaluations covering human judgments, acoustic quality, semantic coherence, and spoken question answering.
The paper investigates both discrete-token and continuous-embedding modeling, and provides training details and evaluation prompts in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Comparisons vary the backbone, training data, adaptation procedure, and speech decoder. The matched S3 baseline is useful but insufficiently specified, and there are no ablations of the cross-attention design, shallow versus deep features, quantization, or learned alignment versus simple pooling or forced alignment.

The approximately 150-bps claim lacks explicit accounting for all decoder inputs, including transcription and speaker embedding. Comparisons with waveform codecs therefore do not establish an equivalent total-bitrate advantage. Reconstruction also trades fidelity for perceptual quality: TASTE has worse WER, ViSQOL, and duration consistency than several baselines.

Evidence for superiority over the matched cascade is weak. Embedding TASLM achieves essentially identical GPT-4o scores (3.16 versus 3.15), lower UTMOS (4.22 versus 4.25), and only a modest human-MOS increase (4.16 versus 4.00). Human evaluation uses just 20 utterances per method; reported dispersions do not establish significance through paired, utterance-level analysis.

Semantic improvements do not establish stronger acoustic understanding. SALMON averages are 60.8 and 57.7, versus 69.0 for expressive Spirit LM, with several subtasks near chance. A text-only model adapted on the same transcripts is needed to distinguish benefits of speech representations from additional textual training.

Technical correctness and reproducibility need attention. Equation 7 uses sigma rather than sigma squared in the Gaussian KL variance term, inconsistent with the stated distribution. Important architectural settings, loss weights, SLM training duration, likelihood-scoring details, and few-shot QA prompts are missing. The advertised code/model/demo links are blank in the supplied manuscript.

The central assumption of sufficiently accurate ASR is untested under transcription errors or challenging audio. Text-aligned editing is supported primarily by a qualitative example, without quantitative evidence of alignment locality or preservation of untouched regions. These gaps leave the method's robustness and claimed generality insufficiently established for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: the sequence-length mismatch between speech and text in joint language modeling. Learning text-aligned acoustic representations through reconstruction is a coherent and potentially useful contribution.

Reconstruction results demonstrate substantial compression while retaining useful acoustic information. At the reported approximately 150 bps, TASTE achieves 0.91 duration consistency and 68.3 MUSHRA, substantially exceeding the text-only baseline's 0.57 and 42.6.

The downstream results are promising: a 1.3B model with 45M fine-tuned parameters outperforms the evaluated larger SLMs on continuation metrics and achieves strong StoryCloze results. Both discrete-token and continuous-embedding modeling are explored.

The evaluation includes human listening tests, multiple objective metrics, ASR-versus-ground-truth ablations, an alternative transcription model for semantic evaluation, and noise robustness experiments. Attention visualizations and shallow-layer analyses provide additional support for the design.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the benefit of the proposed alignment mechanism. Comparisons with existing SLMs differ in backbone, training, and speech decoder. The matched S3 baseline is useful but insufficiently specified and performs poorly; there is no controlled comparison against simple pooled or explicitly word-aligned representations at a comparable rate. Module ablations primarily report teacher-forced top-5 unit accuracy rather than downstream SLM performance.

The claim of surpassing the corresponding cascade system is not convincingly established. TASLM embedding and the same-backbone cascade have essentially identical semantic scores (3.16 versus 3.15), while TASLM has slightly lower UTMOS (4.22 versus 4.25). The human advantage (4.16 versus 4.00) comes from only 20 distinct prompts per method, without a paired significance analysis or confidence interval accounting for repeated listener ratings.

The semantic benchmark gains need a text-only likelihood baseline using the same backbone and ASR transcripts. Otherwise, StoryCloze improvements cannot be attributed specifically to acoustic modeling. Acoustic results are mixed: SALMON accuracy is 60.8/57.7 for the two proposed variants versus 69.0 for Spirit LM Expressive, with several environmental attributes near chance.

The compression comparison needs explicit accounting for all decoder inputs. Reconstruction also uses text and a separate speaker embedding, but the bitrate calculation does not clearly specify speaker-side-information cost or its amortization. Strong speaker similarity therefore does not independently establish that the proposed speech tokens preserve speaker identity. Likewise, the 1.3B parameter comparison excludes the substantial ASR and synthesis components, and no end-to-end computational measurements are provided.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including aggregator and unit-decoder configurations, SLM training duration, loss weights, generation settings, and how text and acoustic scores are combined and normalized for likelihood evaluation. Equation 7 also appears incorrect: the stated Gaussian KL requires a variance term sigma squared, whereas the equation uses sigma. Clarification is needed to distinguish a typographical error from an implementation error.

The strongest alignment and disentanglement claims exceed the evidence. Matching sequence lengths does not itself ensure local acoustic alignment, and the editing demonstration is qualitative rather than a systematic locality evaluation. Appendix A.4 additionally requires word-level grouping, averaging, and replication to reconcile tokenizers; how averaged embeddings map back to discrete RVQ codes is insufficiently explained. These issues weaken the claims of straightforward, heuristic-free alignment and nonredundant paralinguistic encoding.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: aligning speech and text representations to simplify joint language modeling. Text-conditioned aggregation into compact, word-aligned speech representations is a useful and clearly motivated contribution.

Reconstruction results demonstrate a promising compression–quality tradeoff. TASTE achieves 68.3 MUSHRA at approximately 150 bps, compared with 67.6 for Mimi at 1,000 bps, and substantially improves duration consistency over the text-only baseline.

The downstream results provide concrete positive evidence: the 1.3B TASLM models outperform the evaluated TWIST and Spirit LM systems on continuation quality and StoryCloze despite using only LoRA adaptation.

The appendix strengthens the evaluation through ASR-versus-ground-truth comparisons, an alternative evaluation ASR, controlled noise experiments, detailed benchmark breakdowns, and reported variability.
weaknesses: The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the benefit of the proposed alignment mechanism. Comparisons with pretrained SLMs differ in base language model, training, and synthesis components. The matched S3 baseline is useful but performs unusually poorly and lacks sufficient implementation and tuning details. A matched joint model using forced-aligned word pooling or another simple aggregation method would establish whether the proposed tokenizer offers an advantage over simpler alternatives.

Claims of outperforming the corresponding cascade system are stronger than the evidence. TASLM embedding and the matched cascade score 3.16 versus 3.15 on GPT-4o, while TASLM has slightly lower UTMOS, 4.22 versus 4.25. Human MOS improves from 4.00 to 4.16, but evaluation covers only 20 distinct samples per method. Reported standard deviations do not establish the significance of this difference; paired, sample-level uncertainty is needed.

Acoustic modeling results are substantially less convincing than semantic results. SALMON accuracy is 60.8 for the token model and 57.7 for the embedding model, versus 69.0 for Spirit LM Expressive. Several environmental consistency tasks approach chance. Averaging SALMON and StoryCloze into one overall score obscures this tradeoff and weakens broad claims about preserving paralinguistic information.

The practical alignment procedure is less straightforward than the main presentation suggests. Appendix A.4 averages ASR-token embeddings by word and repeats them across LLM subwords. It does not clearly explain how averaged embeddings map back to discrete RVQ codes or how generated subword-level predictions are reconciled for decoding. These details are central to reproducing both model variants.

Important technical and reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent. Equation 7 uses sigma where the stated Gaussian KL requires sigma squared. The manuscript does not adequately specify likelihood scoring for the continuous embedding model, loss coefficients, aggregator and decoder configurations, or downstream training duration. The promised code/model URL is absent from the supplied manuscript.

The efficiency and representation claims need tighter qualification. The bitrate accounting does not clearly include the auxiliary speaker embedding, and the 1.3B parameter comparison excludes additional pipeline components. No end-to-end latency or compute measurements establish practical efficiency. Likewise, attention visualizations and a qualitative token-swapping example support alignment but do not establish that the speech representation avoids redundant lexical information.

strengths: TASTE addresses a meaningful problem: reducing the length mismatch between speech and text representations for joint language modeling. Text-conditioned aggregation with a reconstruction objective is a useful contribution beyond simply adopting an existing speech codec.

The reconstruction results provide concrete evidence that the speech representation retains useful information. Compared with text-only reconstruction, TASTE improves duration consistency from 0.57 to 0.91 and human MUSHRA from 42.6 to 68.3 while operating at a low reported bitrate.

The downstream results are promising: the 1.3B TASLM substantially outperforms TWIST and Spirit LM on continuation evaluations and achieves strong StoryCloze results using LoRA. Including a cascade baseline and a same-backbone S3 baseline strengthens the evaluation.

The appendix adds useful checks, including ASR versus ground-truth transcripts, an alternative evaluation ASR, noise robustness, attention visualizations, and shallow-layer analysis. The paper also acknowledges limitations involving streaming, multilingual speech, and non-lexical events.
weaknesses: The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the proposed alignment mechanism as the source of downstream gains. Comparisons with published SLMs differ in backbone, training data, and synthesis components, while the S3 joint-modeling baseline is insufficiently specified. A matched comparison against forced-alignment pooling or another compression strategy, plus a text-only model adapted on the same transcripts, would better establish the contribution.

The practical alignment procedure introduces an important unresolved technical detail. Appendix A.4 averages already-quantized embeddings within words and repeats these averages across LLM subwords, but does not explain how the resulting vectors map back to valid RVQ codes for TASLMtoken or how generated embeddings are converted back for decoding. This also qualifies the main-text claim of straightforward one-to-one alignment without heuristics.

The strongest perceptual claims have limited statistical support. Human evaluation uses only 20 utterances per method, despite collecting multiple ratings per utterance. Reported standard deviations do not establish whether the 4.16 versus 4.00 MOS difference over the same-backbone cascade is significant. The claim that TASLM surpasses its underlying text-based system therefore needs more evidence.

The compression comparison requires clearer accounting and qualification. Reconstruction uses text and an additional speaker embedding, but the paper does not explicitly itemize their contribution to the reported bitrate or resolve the rate implications of word-level embedding averaging. Moreover, TASTE has worse WER and duration consistency than several codecs; high predicted MOS alone does not demonstrate comparable reconstruction fidelity.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing or inconsistent: aggregator and unit-decoder configurations, latent-loss weights, SLM training duration, decoding settings, and the likelihood scoring rule for continuous embeddings. Equation 7 uses sigma where the stated Gaussian KL requires sigma squared. The abstract also announces code and models without supplying a usable link.

Evidence for broadly preserving paralinguistic information is mixed. Duration editing is demonstrated qualitatively, without systematic transfer measurements, and TASLM's SALMON performance trails Spirit LM Expressive, especially on sentiment and environmental attributes. These results support a narrower claim than general preservation of speech characteristics.
